screens.title: Configuring Basic iBGP Peering and Route Reflectors
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on internal BGP — the mechanism routers inside the same Autonomous System use to share external routes. You will learn why iBGP is necessary when multiple edge routers receive different external prefixes, how the iBGP split-horizon rule forces a full-mesh in naive designs, and why loopback-sourced sessions and an IGP are essential to make those sessions resilient. We will then introduce Route Reflectors, which allow a central router to reflect routes for a cluster of clients and dramatically reduce the number of iBGP sessions you must manage. A concrete configuration example using Junos is included, showing loopback-based peering and the exact statements used to mark neighbors as route-reflector clients and to set the cluster ID. You will also learn common mistakes: missing IGP reachability for loopbacks, forgetting local-address, and misconfiguring client/server roles. By the end of this lesson you will be able to set up basic iBGP session between two routers, convert one router to a Route Reflector server, and verify sessions with the recommended show commands. Think about your own network: where would a Route Reflector reduce complexity, and which loopback addresses would you choose as stable identifiers?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Overview
Configuring Basic iBGP Peering and Route Reflectors
Understand how internal BGP distributes external routes inside an AS and how Route Reflectors solve the full-mesh problem.
In this lesson

Establish iBGP sessions using loopbacks, verify IGP reachability, and configure a Route Reflector with clients using Junos commands and best practices.

Why it matters

As networks grow, managing many iBGP sessions becomes error-prone. Route Reflectors let you scale while preserving route visibility.

Explore Key Topics
iBGP Necessity
Why internal distribution of external routes is required for consistent forwarding.
Loopbacks & IGP
Using loopback addresses and ensuring IGP reachability for stable BGP sessions.
Route Reflectors
How RRs break the full-mesh and the role of cluster IDs and client flags.
Topology Concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Scenario
Multiple edge routers receive different external prefixes. iBGP is used so internal routers can make forwarding decisions based on a consistent set of external routes.
Practical step
Use loopbacks as BGP local-address and verify loopback reachability via OSPF or another IGP before bringing up iBGP.
Key takeaway
Route Reflectors reduce iBGP session count and simplify operations, but their design must avoid new loops or reachability holes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will achieve four practical competencies that prepare you to operate and scale iBGP inside an Autonomous System. First, you will explain why iBGP is needed to distribute external routes within an AS and why the iBGP split-horizon rule creates a full-mesh requirement. Being able to articulate the root cause — split-horizon — helps you choose correct scaling strategies. Second, you will configure basic iBGP peering in Junos between routers that use loopback interfaces. This includes setting loopback addresses, the routing-options autonomous-system, the BGP group with type internal, and local-address so the session is sourced from the loopback. Third, you will describe the Route Reflector concept: how a server reflects client routes and how the cluster identifier avoids reflection loops. Knowing the exact effect of route-reflector-client flags prevents accidental topology issues. Each objective links practice to reason: you will configure, verify, and reason about why each line matters. This will leave you ready to set up a three-router lab and troubleshoot common iBGP mistakes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on practical verification, common pitfalls, and the lab steps that lock in the skills. You will practice configuring loopback interfaces and the autonomous-system statement, setting BGP groups with type internal, and using local-address to force the session to originate from the loopback. Equally important is verification: you will use commands equivalent to show bgp summary and show bgp neighbor to confirm sessions are Established, and show route to confirm that loopback addresses are present in the routing table. You will also learn the typical failure modes: missing IGP advertisement of loopbacks, forgetting local-address which causes sessions to use physical interface addresses, and incorrectly applying route-reflector-client flags on clients rather than on the server. Each hands-on step in the lab reinforces the configuration explanation; for example, after configuring R1 as a Route Reflector and R2 and R3 as clients, you will validate that routes learned from R2 are reflected to R3 via the RR. These verification routines are the same steps you will use in production troubleshooting.

keyIdea.title: Practice focus
keyIdea.text: Configuration is only complete when you verify IGP reachability, BGP session state, and route reflection behavior using show commands.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Practice & Troubleshooting
Lab checklist
  1. Create loopbacks on each router and assign /32 addresses used as local-address.
  2. Ensure loopbacks are advertised in OSPF or another IGP so they are reachable.
  3. Configure BGP group with type internal and neighbors pointing to peer loopbacks.
  4. Convert one router to a Route Reflector server and set route-reflector-client flags on neighbors.
  5. Verify sessions with show bgp summary and check route reflection with show route protocol bgp.
Quick verification commands (conceptual)
show bgp summary — confirm Established state for all iBGP neighbors.
show route <peer-loopback-ip> — confirm loopback reachability in the IGP.
show route protocol bgp — confirm reflected routes and origin.

screens.title: Why iBGP is necessary inside an AS
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining the problem: when several edge routers peer with different external Autonomous Systems, each edge learns a different set of external prefixes via eBGP. If internal routers only relied on IGP or partial knowledge, forwarding decisions could be inconsistent — packets might be sent to an edge router that doesn't know the best external path. iBGP exists so that routes learned from eBGP on one edge can be shared with every BGP-speaking router inside the same Autonomous System. That consistent view lets internal devices make correct forwarding decisions for traffic destined outside the AS. A useful mental model is to think of iBGP as a distribution layer for externally learned information. Concretely, imagine Router A peers with ISP-1 and learns prefix 203.0.113.0/24, while Router B peers with ISP-2 and learns 198.51.100.0/24. Without iBGP, an internal router might only know one of those prefixes and forward traffic incorrectly. A common misconception is to assume an IGP will distribute these external prefixes automatically; it won't unless you inject them, and BGP holds routing attributes and policy that IGPs do not replicate. Key takeaway: iBGP preserves routing policy and attributes across the AS so internal routers can make correct decisions. How would you verify that an internal router has learned both external prefixes via BGP rather than via static routes?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: iBGP enables consistent distribution of external BGP-learned routes within an Autonomous System so internal routers can make correct forwarding decisions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › iBGP Necessity
Concept
iBGP distributes eBGP-learned routes within an AS so all BGP speakers share the same external routing information and attributes.
Concrete example
If Router A learns 203.0.113.0/24 from ISP-1 and Router B learns 198.51.100.0/24 from ISP-2, iBGP ensures a transit router sees both prefixes and can forward accordingly.
Common misconception
Do not assume an IGP automatically provides BGP attributes or policies. BGP conveys attributes like local preference and AS-path that influence path selection and are not replicated by an IGP without explicit redistribution.
Key takeaway
iBGP is a distribution mechanism for external routes and their policies; it is required when multiple edge peers exist.
Verification scenario
Use show route protocol bgp and show bgp summary on internal routers to confirm prefixes are learned via BGP with appropriate attributes. Confirm that the AS-path and next-hop match expected values from the edge peers.
Analogy
Think of iBGP as a bulletin board inside the AS where edge routers pin external routes so everyone sees the same announcements and rules for choosing a path.
Check your understanding
If an internal router lacks a specific external prefix, is the likely issue missing iBGP distribution or a policy filtering the prefix? Use show route to determine if it was learned at all.

screens.title: iBGP split-horizon and the full-mesh implication
screens.narratorSegment: Here we examine the split-horizon rule and derive the full-mesh math. The split-horizon rule in iBGP states that a BGP speaker will not advertise a route learned from one iBGP neighbor to another iBGP neighbor. This prevents loops but means that peer-to-peer propagation cannot be done transitively. The consequence is the full-mesh requirement: with N routers, naive iBGP requires N times N minus one divided by two sessions. For small N that is manageable, but for larger N it becomes operationally painful. For example, ten routers need forty-five sessions — each session is a TCP connection, configuration entry, and monitoring point. A concrete misconception to avoid is thinking that simply establishing BGP neighbors on an IGP path solves the split-horizon constraint; it does not. The split-horizon rule is part of BGP's semantics. The usual mitigation strategies are Route Reflectors or confederations. Route Reflectors allow a single server to reflect client routes to other clients and thereby bypass the split-horizon inside a cluster; confederations split the AS into sub-ASes so fewer sessions are needed across boundaries. To decide between options, consider operational complexity, policy control, and loop risk. Reflect for a moment: how many iBGP sessions would your network need if you had eight core routers?

keyIdea.title: Split-horizon consequence
keyIdea.text: iBGP's split-horizon prevents transitive advertisement between iBGP peers, producing a full-mesh requirement that scales poorly without Route Reflectors or confederations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Split-horizon & Full-mesh
Rule
A BGP speaker does not advertise routes learned via iBGP to other iBGP peers. That rule prevents loops but blocks transitive propagation inside an AS.
Full-mesh formula
Sessions = N * (N - 1) / 2
Example: N = 10 → 10 * 9 / 2 = 45 sessions.
Misconception
Establishing an IGP path doesn't change split-horizon semantics. IGP provides reachability for loopbacks, but BGP still enforces its advertisement rules.
Mitigation options
Route Reflectors
Use an RR server to reflect routes between clients and reduce session count dramatically.
Confederations
Split a large AS into sub-ASes to limit full-mesh within each confederation and control policy across boundaries.
Check
If you have eight core routers, how many sessions are required by a full mesh? (Answer: 8 * 7 / 2 = 28.)

screens.title: Using loopback interfaces for iBGP peering
screens.narratorSegment: Loopback interfaces are the recommended source and destination addresses for iBGP sessions because they are virtual, always-up, and unaffected by physical interface state. To use loopbacks you must make sure the loopback addresses are reachable by the other router; this is done through an IGP such as OSPF or IS-IS. A common pitfall is to configure local-address to the loopback but forget to advertise that loopback into the IGP — the BGP session will remain in Active because the TCP connection cannot be established to the loopback. The Junos configuration pattern is straightforward: configure lo0 with a /32, set routing-options autonomous-system, then in protocols bgp create a group with type internal, list the neighbor loopback IP, and set local-address to your own loopback. Here's a minimal working example between Router A and Router B. After applying this configuration, verify the IGP has learned the peer loopback and then watch show bgp summary to confirm the session reaches Established. Misconception to avoid: local-address is optional for eBGP but important for loopback-based iBGP, so always specify it when you use loopbacks. Now, examine the example and notice how few lines are required to form a stable iBGP session when reachability is correct.

keyIdea.title: Loopback best practice
keyIdea.text: Use loopback addresses as BGP local-address for stability, and ensure those loopbacks are advertised in your IGP before expecting sessions to come up.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Loopbacks & IGP
Junos example — Router A
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.100.1/32
set routing-options autonomous-system 65000
set protocols bgp group IBGP_PEERS type internal
set protocols bgp group IBGP_PEERS neighbor 192.168.100.2
set protocols bgp group IBGP_PEERS local-address 192.168.100.1
Junos example — Router B
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.100.2/32
set routing-options autonomous-system 65000
set protocols bgp group IBGP_PEERS type internal
set protocols bgp group IBGP_PEERS neighbor 192.168.100.1
set protocols bgp group IBGP_PEERS local-address 192.168.100.2
Verification steps
1) Ensure the IGP advertises both loopbacks. 2) On each router run show route <peer-loopback> to confirm reachability. 3) Run show bgp summary and expect Established state. If Active, check IGP and local-address configuration.

screens.title: Route Reflector concept and cluster identifiers
screens.narratorSegment: A Route Reflector is a BGP speaker configured to reflect routes learned from its clients to other clients, thereby bypassing the iBGP split-horizon limitation within that cluster. The RR becomes a central distribution point: clients peer only with the RR instead of forming a full mesh. The RR configuration marks specific neighbors as route-reflector-client and typically sets a cluster identifier, which is often the RR's router ID or loopback. The cluster ID is important because it helps avoid reflection loops when multiple RRs exist — the RR adds the cluster ID when reflecting routes, and other RRs use it to detect and discard reflected routes that would create duplicates or loops. A common misconception is believing that marking a neighbor as a route-reflector-client is required on the client side; it is not. The server configures that flag. Reflectors simplify session topology, but they add an architectural responsibility: a poorly designed RR cluster can create routing loops or blackholes if reachability to the RR or cluster IDs is inconsistent. As an example, when Router RR learns a prefix from client C, it reflects that prefix to client D; the reflected route will carry cluster information to avoid bouncing back. Consider how you would place RRs to minimize single points of failure while avoiding overly complex reflection hierarchies.

keyIdea.title: Route Reflector role
keyIdea.text: An RR reflects client routes to other clients and uses a cluster ID to avoid reflection loops when multiple RRs are present.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Route Reflector Concept
How reflection works
An RR receives a route from client A and advertises it to client B even though the route was learned via iBGP. That behavior bypasses the split-horizon rule inside the cluster so clients don't need full-mesh peers with each other.
Cluster ID
Assign a cluster identifier to detect and prevent reflection loops across multiple RRs. Use a stable value such as the RR loopback or router ID.
Operational note
Only the RR server needs to mark neighbors as route-reflector-client. Clients simply peer with the RR and do not require special client-side settings.
Design caution
A single RR can become a bottleneck or single point of failure; consider multiple RRs with different cluster IDs and ensure consistent reachability to avoid blackholes.

screens.title: Configuring a Juniper Route Reflector server
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through the Junos configuration required to make a router act as a Route Reflector server. The important pieces are: set the BGP group type to internal, list neighbors that are clients and specify family inet unicast route-reflector-client for each client, set local-address to the RR loopback, and set a cluster identifier so reflections are tagged with a stable ID. The cluster statement is optional but recommended when you run multiple RRs so they can detect previously reflected routes. In the example below R1 becomes the RR with loopback 10.0.0.1 and clients at 10.0.0.2 and 10.0.0.3. After configuration, verify with show bgp group to confirm the group contains the neighbors and show bgp summary to ensure sessions are Established. A frequent error is forgetting to include family inet unicast or mistyping the route-reflector-client option; such mistakes cause the RR to behave like a normal iBGP peer and the full-mesh problem persists. Practice by applying the provided commands in a lab and then advertising a test prefix from a client; observe at another client that the prefix appears via the RR. What verification output will confirm the prefix was reflected rather than learned via eBGP?

keyIdea.title: RR server config
keyIdea.text: On the RR: mark neighbors with route-reflector-client, set local-address to loopback, and set a cluster ID to tag reflections and avoid loops.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Route Reflector Server
RR server example — R1
# Assume lo0 is configured and AS is set
set protocols bgp group IBGP_CLIENTS type internal
set protocols bgp group IBGP_CLIENTS neighbor 10.0.0.2 family inet unicast route-reflector-client
set protocols bgp group IBGP_CLIENTS neighbor 10.0.0.3 family inet unicast route-reflector-client
set protocols bgp group IBGP_CLIENTS local-address 10.0.0.1
set protocols bgp group IBGP_CLIENTS cluster 10.0.0.1
After applying these lines, confirm the group lists both neighbors and that each session is Established. If sessions remain down, first verify loopback reachability via your IGP.

screens.title: Configuring Route Reflector clients in Junos
screens.narratorSegment: Client configuration is intentionally simple. A Route Reflector client needs to peer with the RR and set local-address to its loopback so the session originates from a stable address. There is no route-reflector-client statement on the client; marking a neighbor as a client is a server-side action only. The client must still ensure its loopback is reachable via the IGP. Practically, configure lo0, set the autonomous-system, then under protocols bgp create a group with type internal, list the RR loopback as the neighbor, and set local-address to the client's loopback. After the session establishes, advertise a test prefix and confirm it is visible on other clients via the RR. A common mistake is pointing the neighbor to a non-reachable IP or using a physical interface address without proper IGP advertisement, which prevents the session from establishing. When verifying, run show bgp summary and show route protocol bgp on a peer client to confirm the prefix was reflected and carries the expected attributes. Reflect on this: why does the client not need special RR flags, and what does that reduce in terms of configuration burden?

keyIdea.title: RR client config
keyIdea.text: Clients only peer with the RR and set their local-address to a loopback. The server marks clients; clients do not need special flags.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Route Reflector Client
Client example — R2
# Assume lo0 and AS configured
set protocols bgp group IBGP_TO_RR type internal
set protocols bgp group IBGP_TO_RR local-address 10.0.0.2
set protocols bgp group IBGP_TO_RR neighbor 10.0.0.1 # Peer with RR
Operational checklist
1) Confirm loopback is in the IGP. 2) Confirm show bgp summary reports Established. 3) Advertise a prefix and confirm it appears on other clients via show route protocol bgp.

screens.title: Common iBGP mistakes and their fixes
screens.narratorSegment: In production you will repeatedly encounter a small set of predictable errors. Recognizing them quickly saves time. The first common mistake is lack of IGP reachability for loopbacks. Symptoms: BGP sessions stuck in Active. Fix: ensure loopbacks are included in the IGP or add static routes temporarily for lab work, then re-run show route to confirm reachability. The second mistake is missing local-address. Symptoms: sessions use a physical interface address, mismatch with neighbor configuration, or unexpected source addresses leading to TCP resets. Fix: add local-address referencing the loopback and re-establish the session. The third mistake is trying to advertise iBGP-learned routes to another iBGP peer without a Route Reflector or confederation; this will silently fail because of split-horizon. Fix: introduce an RR or redesign with confederations. The fourth mistake is misconfiguring route-reflector-client flags on the wrong side; only the server should carry that flag. When troubleshooting, follow a checklist: confirm IGP reachability, confirm the configured neighbor IPs match intended loopbacks, check local-address presence, and then inspect show bgp summary. These steps will usually reveal the root cause. Practice walking through these checks in your lab until they become routine.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Common Mistakes
Mistake: IGP not advertising loopbacks
Symptom: BGP stuck in Active. Fix: add loopbacks to OSPF/IS-IS or static routes and confirm with show route <loopback>.
Mistake: Missing local-address
Symptom: TCP source mismatch. Fix: set local-address to the loopback on both peers when using loopback-based peering.
Mistake: Split-horizon violation attempt
Symptom: Routes not forwarded between iBGP peers. Fix: use Route Reflectors or confederations; you cannot advertise iBGP-learned routes to another iBGP peer directly.
Mistake: Client/server flag misplacement
Symptom: RR doesn't reflect routes. Fix: apply route-reflector-client on the RR config for each client; clients require only a normal neighbor statement.
Pro tip

When troubleshooting, start with reachability to the loopback, then local-address, then BGP group settings. These checks solve the majority of lab issues.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: three-router lab with a Route Reflector
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walkthrough ties the concepts together. The scenario uses three routers in AS 65000: R1, R2, and R3. First, configure loopbacks on all routers and advertise them in OSPF or your chosen IGP so each loopback is reachable. Next, form iBGP peering between R1 and R2 using loopbacks and local-address — this is the full-mesh step to validate baseline behavior. Then add R3 and convert R1 to a Route Reflector server by creating a BGP group IBGP_RR, setting local-address to R1's loopback, listing R2 and R3 as neighbors, and marking them with family inet unicast route-reflector-client and setting cluster to R1's loopback. On R2 and R3, configure a simple iBGP neighbor pointing to R1 with local-address as their loopbacks. Verification steps: show bgp summary on each router to confirm Established, show route protocol bgp to see reflected prefixes on clients, and on R1 run show bgp group IBGP_RR to inspect RR client state. A concrete expected outcome is that a prefix advertised from R2 will appear on R3 via R1, demonstrating reflection. A common test failure is forgetting the IGP advertisement for loopbacks; always confirm that first. After the lab, reflect: how many sessions did you reduce by introducing the RR compared to a full-mesh?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Three-router Lab
Starter Junos snippets (R1, R2, R3)
# R1 (RR) Lo0: 10.0.0.1
set routing-options autonomous-system 65000
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.1/32
set protocols bgp group IBGP_RR type internal
set protocols bgp group IBGP_RR local-address 10.0.0.1
set protocols bgp group IBGP_RR neighbor 10.0.0.2 family inet unicast route-reflector-client
set protocols bgp group IBGP_RR neighbor 10.0.0.3 family inet unicast route-reflector-client
set protocols bgp group IBGP_RR cluster 10.0.0.1

# R2 Lo0: 10.0.0.2
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.2/32
set routing-options autonomous-system 65000
set protocols bgp group IBGP_TO_RR type internal
set protocols bgp group IBGP_TO_RR local-address 10.0.0.2
set protocols bgp group IBGP_TO_RR neighbor 10.0.0.1

# R3 Lo0: 10.0.0.3 (similar to R2)
Verification: run show bgp summary, show bgp group IBGP_RR on R1, and show route protocol bgp on clients to observe reflected routes. If you succeed, R3 will see prefixes advertised by R2 without a direct R2-R3 BGP session.
Key Takeaway

The lab demonstrates how an RR reduces session count while preserving route visibility. Always verify IGP reachability before troubleshooting BGP sessions.

screens.title: Assessment and verification scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: To verify mastery, two assessment scenarios highlight the core reasoning and operational checks. First, the math and rationale question: given five core routers in an AS, how many iBGP sessions would a full mesh require, and why would you choose Route Reflectors? The calculation is five times four divided by two equals ten sessions, and the reason is scalability — Route Reflectors reduce configuration and session overhead. Second, an operational troubleshooting question: a BGP session between two routers using loopbacks is stuck in Active though BGP configuration looks correct. The most probable cause is missing IGP reachability for the peer loopback. The verification steps are to run show route for the peer loopback, confirm it is installed via OSPF or the chosen IGP, ensure local-address is configured correctly, then re-check show bgp summary. When grading these tasks, expect the learner to explain both the reason and the concrete verification command sequences. A useful misconception to catch is thinking that tcp connectivity between devices means the loopback is reachable; you must confirm the route in the routing table. End with this reflective question: after running the verification commands, what evidence convinces you the session is now correct?

Question 1 (calculation and rationale)
If there are 5 routers, full-mesh sessions = 5*(5-1)/2 = 10. Why choose Route Reflectors? To reduce session counts and simplify configuration while preserving route visibility.
Question 2 (troubleshooting)

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These three core concepts summarize the chapter. First, iBGP is BGP peering inside a single Autonomous System used to distribute external routes so internal routers make consistent forwarding decisions. Second, the iBGP full-mesh requirement arises from the split-horizon rule that prevents a BGP speaker from advertising an iBGP-learned route to another iBGP peer; this causes N*(N-1)/2 sessions for N routers. Third, loopback interfaces are the recommended source addresses for iBGP because they are stable, but they require IGP reachability before BGP sessions can establish. Keep these definitions in mind as they drive configuration and design choices. When you plan a deployment, ask yourself which routers must see all external prefixes, whether an RR reduces operational load, and whether loopbacks are reachable via the IGP. These checks prevent the most common operational failures.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Key Concepts
iBGP
BGP between routers in the same AS to distribute external routes and preserve policy attributes.
Full-Mesh
Every iBGP speaker peers with every other: N*(N-1)/2 sessions due to split-horizon limitations.
Loopback Interface
Stable /32 interface used for BGP local-address; must be reachable via an IGP for sessions to form.
Summary
Use loopback-based iBGP with careful IGP planning and consider Route Reflectors to scale while preserving route visibility and policy.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: These three compact reminders help when you operate or troubleshoot iBGP. First, always verify IGP reachability for loopbacks before blaming BGP; a session stuck in Active is often an IGP problem. Second, remember to set local-address on loopback-sourced sessions so the TCP handshake uses the expected source address. Third, Route Reflectors must be designed carefully: the server configures route-reflector-client and a cluster ID, and you must avoid creating single points of failure or inconsistent cluster identifiers that can produce reflection loops. Together these checks address most operational errors and keep your iBGP deployment stable. When you next set up iBGP, use this quick checklist: loopbacks configured and advertised, local-address set, BGP groups correct, and show commands confirming Established and reflected routes. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on internal BGP — the mechanism routers inside the same Autonomous System use to share external routes. You will learn why iBGP is necessary when multiple edge routers receive different external prefixes, how the iBGP split-horizon rule forces a full-mesh in naive designs, and why loopback-sourced sessions and an IGP are essential to make those sessions resilient. We will then introduce Route Reflectors, which allow a central router to reflect routes for a cluster of clients and dramatically reduce the number of iBGP sessions you must manage. A concrete configuration example using Junos is included, showing loopback-based peering and the exact statements used to mark neighbors as route-reflector clients and to set the cluster ID. You will also learn common mistakes: missing IGP reachability for loopbacks, forgetting local-address, and misconfiguring client/server roles. By the end of this lesson you will be able to set up basic iBGP session between two routers, convert one router to a Route Reflector server, and verify sessions with the recommended show commands. Think about your own network: where would a Route Reflector reduce complexity, and which loopback addresses would you choose as stable identifiers?

In this chapter you will achieve four practical competencies that prepare you to operate and scale iBGP inside an Autonomous System. First, you will explain why iBGP is needed to distribute external routes within an AS and why the iBGP split-horizon rule creates a full-mesh requirement. Being able to articulate the root cause — split-horizon — helps you choose correct scaling strategies. Second, you will configure basic iBGP peering in Junos between routers that use loopback interfaces. This includes setting loopback addresses, the routing-options autonomous-system, the BGP group with type internal, and local-address so the session is sourced from the loopback. Third, you will describe the Route Reflector concept: how a server reflects client routes and how the cluster identifier avoids reflection loops. Knowing the exact effect of route-reflector-client flags prevents accidental topology issues. Each objective links practice to reason: you will configure, verify, and reason about why each line matters. This will leave you ready to set up a three-router lab and troubleshoot common iBGP mistakes.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical verification, common pitfalls, and the lab steps that lock in the skills. You will practice configuring loopback interfaces and the autonomous-system statement, setting BGP groups with type internal, and using local-address to force the session to originate from the loopback. Equally important is verification: you will use commands equivalent to show bgp summary and show bgp neighbor to confirm sessions are Established, and show route to confirm that loopback addresses are present in the routing table. You will also learn the typical failure modes: missing IGP advertisement of loopbacks, forgetting local-address which causes sessions to use physical interface addresses, and incorrectly applying route-reflector-client flags on clients rather than on the server. Each hands-on step in the lab reinforces the configuration explanation; for example, after configuring R1 as a Route Reflector and R2 and R3 as clients, you will validate that routes learned from R2 are reflected to R3 via the RR. These verification routines are the same steps you will use in production troubleshooting.

Start by defining the problem: when several edge routers peer with different external Autonomous Systems, each edge learns a different set of external prefixes via eBGP. If internal routers only relied on IGP or partial knowledge, forwarding decisions could be inconsistent — packets might be sent to an edge router that doesn't know the best external path. iBGP exists so that routes learned from eBGP on one edge can be shared with every BGP-speaking router inside the same Autonomous System. That consistent view lets internal devices make correct forwarding decisions for traffic destined outside the AS. A useful mental model is to think of iBGP as a distribution layer for externally learned information. Concretely, imagine Router A peers with ISP-1 and learns prefix 203.0.113.0/24, while Router B peers with ISP-2 and learns 198.51.100.0/24. Without iBGP, an internal router might only know one of those prefixes and forward traffic incorrectly. A common misconception is to assume an IGP will distribute these external prefixes automatically; it won't unless you inject them, and BGP holds routing attributes and policy that IGPs do not replicate. Key takeaway: iBGP preserves routing policy and attributes across the AS so internal routers can make correct decisions. How would you verify that an internal router has learned both external prefixes via BGP rather than via static routes?

Here we examine the split-horizon rule and derive the full-mesh math. The split-horizon rule in iBGP states that a BGP speaker will not advertise a route learned from one iBGP neighbor to another iBGP neighbor. This prevents loops but means that peer-to-peer propagation cannot be done transitively. The consequence is the full-mesh requirement: with N routers, naive iBGP requires N times N minus one divided by two sessions. For small N that is manageable, but for larger N it becomes operationally painful. For example, ten routers need forty-five sessions — each session is a TCP connection, configuration entry, and monitoring point. A concrete misconception to avoid is thinking that simply establishing BGP neighbors on an IGP path solves the split-horizon constraint; it does not. The split-horizon rule is part of BGP's semantics. The usual mitigation strategies are Route Reflectors or confederations. Route Reflectors allow a single server to reflect client routes to other clients and thereby bypass the split-horizon inside a cluster; confederations split the AS into sub-ASes so fewer sessions are needed across boundaries. To decide between options, consider operational complexity, policy control, and loop risk. Reflect for a moment: how many iBGP sessions would your network need if you had eight core routers?

Loopback interfaces are the recommended source and destination addresses for iBGP sessions because they are virtual, always-up, and unaffected by physical interface state. To use loopbacks you must make sure the loopback addresses are reachable by the other router; this is done through an IGP such as OSPF or IS-IS. A common pitfall is to configure local-address to the loopback but forget to advertise that loopback into the IGP — the BGP session will remain in Active because the TCP connection cannot be established to the loopback. The Junos configuration pattern is straightforward: configure lo0 with a /32, set routing-options autonomous-system, then in protocols bgp create a group with type internal, list the neighbor loopback IP, and set local-address to your own loopback. Here's a minimal working example between Router A and Router B. After applying this configuration, verify the IGP has learned the peer loopback and then watch show bgp summary to confirm the session reaches Established. Misconception to avoid: local-address is optional for eBGP but important for loopback-based iBGP, so always specify it when you use loopbacks. Now, examine the example and notice how few lines are required to form a stable iBGP session when reachability is correct.

A Route Reflector is a BGP speaker configured to reflect routes learned from its clients to other clients, thereby bypassing the iBGP split-horizon limitation within that cluster. The RR becomes a central distribution point: clients peer only with the RR instead of forming a full mesh. The RR configuration marks specific neighbors as route-reflector-client and typically sets a cluster identifier, which is often the RR's router ID or loopback. The cluster ID is important because it helps avoid reflection loops when multiple RRs exist — the RR adds the cluster ID when reflecting routes, and other RRs use it to detect and discard reflected routes that would create duplicates or loops. A common misconception is believing that marking a neighbor as a route-reflector-client is required on the client side; it is not. The server configures that flag. Reflectors simplify session topology, but they add an architectural responsibility: a poorly designed RR cluster can create routing loops or blackholes if reachability to the RR or cluster IDs is inconsistent. As an example, when Router RR learns a prefix from client C, it reflects that prefix to client D; the reflected route will carry cluster information to avoid bouncing back. Consider how you would place RRs to minimize single points of failure while avoiding overly complex reflection hierarchies.

Now we'll walk through the Junos configuration required to make a router act as a Route Reflector server. The important pieces are: set the BGP group type to internal, list neighbors that are clients and specify family inet unicast route-reflector-client for each client, set local-address to the RR loopback, and set a cluster identifier so reflections are tagged with a stable ID. The cluster statement is optional but recommended when you run multiple RRs so they can detect previously reflected routes. In the example below R1 becomes the RR with loopback 10.0.0.1 and clients at 10.0.0.2 and 10.0.0.3. After configuration, verify with show bgp group to confirm the group contains the neighbors and show bgp summary to ensure sessions are Established. A frequent error is forgetting to include family inet unicast or mistyping the route-reflector-client option; such mistakes cause the RR to behave like a normal iBGP peer and the full-mesh problem persists. Practice by applying the provided commands in a lab and then advertising a test prefix from a client; observe at another client that the prefix appears via the RR. What verification output will confirm the prefix was reflected rather than learned via eBGP?

Client configuration is intentionally simple. A Route Reflector client needs to peer with the RR and set local-address to its loopback so the session originates from a stable address. There is no route-reflector-client statement on the client; marking a neighbor as a client is a server-side action only. The client must still ensure its loopback is reachable via the IGP. Practically, configure lo0, set the autonomous-system, then under protocols bgp create a group with type internal, list the RR loopback as the neighbor, and set local-address to the client's loopback. After the session establishes, advertise a test prefix and confirm it is visible on other clients via the RR. A common mistake is pointing the neighbor to a non-reachable IP or using a physical interface address without proper IGP advertisement, which prevents the session from establishing. When verifying, run show bgp summary and show route protocol bgp on a peer client to confirm the prefix was reflected and carries the expected attributes. Reflect on this: why does the client not need special RR flags, and what does that reduce in terms of configuration burden?
